claims.claim: strategy.md commits that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet-generated Applications 'will not be implemented' and that teardown remains a manual per-Application operator action, while the progressive-sync deletion PRD's entire purpose is to ship a deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) that automates ordered deletion of exactly those children — both commitments cannot hold, and note-2 records the disagreement as unowned and undecided.

RFC-001 designs impersonation as a switch that 'can be enabled/disabled only at the system level' applying to all Applications, but T-26271 reports enabling 'the sync impersonation flag' per project in the field, and the platform-call decision (note-1) mandates a per-project rollout gated on the diff fix — the RFC's system-level-only enablement model and the org's decided rollout plan cannot both hold without a design change.

T-26271's reporter cannot understand why CI diffs 'suddenly run with a narrower identity' despite a broad cluster Secret, but RFC-001 explains the symptom exactly: with impersonation enabled, operations execute as the AppProject's destination service account rather than the control-plane credential, so the server-side-apply dry-run behind the diff is authorized against the narrow SA that lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources — the ticket should be read as a designed consequence of the RFC, not a cluster-credential bug.

T-28695 inverts RFC-001's security promise on external clusters: because Server-Side Diff's dry-run is authorized as a real 'patch' and the diff path ignores destinationServiceAccounts, operators must keep granting unbounded write authority to the standing cluster credential — the exact credential RFC-001 set out to narrow — so the RFC's 'least privilege' goal should be read as unmet whenever SSD is enabled.

T-27833's proposed fix (control-plane SA bootstraps namespaces while the impersonated SA syncs everything else) is foreclosed by RFC-001, which explicitly answers that the impersonation service account is determined per Application, never per resource — so the impersonation feature as designed cannot deliver the split T-27833 asks for, and the ticket needs either an RFC amendment or a different mechanism.

The PRD's Risks section says 'No immediate Risks' and its Security section claims no impact, but T-28511 is a live incident against the very deletionOrder feature the PRD specifies: with Reverse deletion, a child app stuck in Progressing blocks the wait-for-full-deletion barrier and the controller loops deleting and re-creating the Application — field evidence already falsifies the PRD's risk assessment before the PRD is even approved.

T-24578 asks for hydrator support in ApplicationSets specifically to get controlled destroy ordering, which is the same demand the deletion PRD serves — but strategy.md's declaration that ordered deletion of ApplicationSet children is out of scope blocks both work items at once, so the strategy line is the single decision gating two otherwise unrelated tickets and neither document acknowledges the other.

T-9095's request (let UI actions like pod deletion ride on the user's existing Kubernetes RBAC) is precisely the user/group impersonation that RFC-001 explicitly deferred ('support to impersonate users or groups can be added in future'), so T-9095 should be read as the demand signal for that deferred RFC extension rather than as an unrelated dashboard feature.

Enabling the RFC-002 hydrator on repositories governed by progressive sync makes rollouts unable to converge: every hydration cycle lands a fresh machine commit on the sync branch, T-27949's pilot observed each such commit picked up as a source change, and note-2 confirmed each hydrator push restarts the RollingSync wave from the top — a combination hazard stated in no design document, since neither RFC-002 nor the PRD mentions progressive sync interaction at all.

The hydrator will amplify T-27875's auto-sync race from an edge case into a common failure: the bug fires exactly when a new commit lands on the watched branch while a previous sync is in flight, and RFC-002's design multiplies commit frequency on sync branches (one machine commit per dry commit per environment branch, batched across many apps), so hydrator adoption raises the probability of apps silently sticking OutOfSync indefinitely — a coupling neither document states.

The org's push-to-stage deployment path rests on an unowned component: RFC-002 delegates promotion to 'some external system', note-1 records that this system is still an ownerless shell script, and T-26443 already documents the failure mode when the promoter lags — auto-sync deploying whatever stale manifests the stage branch last held — so a silent promoter outage translates directly into production running old state with nobody accountable.

T-27327's rollback design (push a git-checkout commit directly to the sync branch, bypassing staging) collides with T-28239's signing plan: once operators enforce signature verification on the hydrated branch — the step T-28239 explicitly instructs — any rollback commit not produced by the signing commit server gets rejected, meaning rollback breaks precisely in the security-hardened configuration and precisely during an incident; the rollback commit also violates RFC-002's invariant that every deployed change corresponds to a current dry commit, which can mislead any promoter reading hydrator.metadata.

The PRD's Reverse strategy introduces an indefinite blocking wait (each Application must fully delete before the next starts) while requesting zero observability, and the surrounding evidence shows nobody could see it stall in production: T-27846 documents that progressive sync already cannot answer 'my sync is not starting, which Applications is it waiting for', and T-27949's incident produced no logs because transitions log below warn level — so a stuck deletion wave would emit no metric and no log, discoverable only by a human staring at the UI.

RFC-002 pitches the hydrator to organizations 'with strong requirements around change auditing', yet nothing attests the machine authorship it introduces: T-28239 establishes that hydrated commits are pushed unsigned, and RFC-002 leaves branch protection for hydrated branches an open question while requiring a repository-write GitHub App secret — so anyone holding that credential can author deploy-triggering commits indistinguishable from the hydrator's own, and the audit trail the RFC advertises cannot distinguish machine-written from human-forged history until signing lands.

T-28927 proposes promoting Progressive Sync to Stable — a status defined as 'tested and validated... mature, backwards compatible' — while T-27949 (spec-only changes silently never sync) and T-28511 (delete/recreate loop) are open correctness bugs, the incident review just imposed operational bans (AllAtOnce-only manual deletion, no hydrator pilots on progressive sync), and the deletionOrder API surface it would freeze is still contested between the PRD and strategy.md; stabilizing now would lock in backwards-compatibility guarantees on behavior the org itself does not trust yet.

proposals.change: Add the root cause established on the platform sync call: with impersonation enabled, the diff runs as the destination service account, which does not hold patch on cluster-scoped resources — the broad cluster Secret credential is not involved, so stop investigating it.
proposals.citedLine: the CI diff failures (the missing-permissions one, T-26271) got root-caused on the call: with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch on cluster-scoped stuff. someone should note the root cause on that ticket so the reporter stops chasing the cluster secret.

proposals.change: Mark the History & Rollback hydrator work as deprioritized to next quarter; the dev pair assigned to it moves to the progressive sync deletion work instead.
proposals.citedLine: hydrator rollback work (the history & rollback ticket, T-27327) is deprioritized to next quarter. dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead. ticket should say so.

proposals.change: Record the interim restriction from the incident review: hydrator pilot repositories must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists, because each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave.
proposals.citedLine: the wave-restart thing on hydrated repos: we confirmed each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce. the pilot ticket (T-27949) should carry that restriction so the next team doesn't trip it.

proposals.change: Note that the delete/recreate loop was reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order configured, and record the interim mitigation: switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before manually deleting any child Application, until the controller fix lands.
proposals.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

deltas.body: Impersonation rolls out behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide, and no project enables it until the diff identity problem is fixed.
deltas.citedLine: impersonation rollout: we decided it goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed. that's a real decision, not a maybe.

deltas.body: Standing operational practice: before manually deleting any child Application of an ApplicationSet, switch the ApplicationSet's deletion strategy to AllAtOnce; this remains the rule until the controller fix for the delete/recreate loop lands.
deltas.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

deltas.body: Hydrator pilot repositories must not use progressive sync until a debounce for hydrator pushes exists, because each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave.
deltas.citedLine: the wave-restart thing on hydrated repos: we confirmed each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce. the pilot ticket (T-27949) should carry that restriction so the next team doesn't trip it.
